metadata.title: Old MANALI Food Tour l Sabali + Lazy Dog + Dylan’s + Corner House + Chopstick + Chha Meat + Kukkad
metadata.description:
We went on an Old Manali food tour with our host, Khushboo Barry, an entrepreneur who also runs a homestay in the valley. Manali, with its snow-draped peaks, pine-covered slopes, and the Beas River rushing through, has long been a travelers’ haven. Beyond the views and mountain air, the food scene here is equally fascinating, shaped by locals, long-term settlers, and visitors from around the world who have made it their home.

Our first stop was Sabali Bakery, started by a Sudanese man and his wife. Over the years it has grown into one of the most happening spots in Old Manali, especially popular with the young international crowd. The menu is colorful, eclectic, and full of energy. We tried a refreshing chia pudding, a soft bagel with cream cheese, and a delicate matcha tart, each reflecting the café’s global spirit.

From there we walked to Dylan’s Coffee House, an iconic name in Old Manali. The café has a loyal following of travelers who return again and again for its cozy atmosphere and irresistible bakes. We had the chance to meet one of the founders, who shared their journey of starting the café and nurturing it into the landmark it is today. Their legendary secret cookies lived up to the reputation, and the strong bulletproof coffee gave us just the right kick to carry on with our day.

Next on the trail was The Lazy Dog Café, where we were welcomed by its owner, once a TV journalist, who traded the newsroom for the warmth of hospitality. He shared stories of how the café took shape along the banks of the river. The food here was exceptional—perfectly cooked rainbow trout fish, a fresh smoked chicken salad, and sushi rolls that brought a touch of Japanese finesse to the mountains.

The Cornerhouse Restaurant and Café was our next stop, run by Siddharth, a young entrepreneur and trained chef. His menu reflects both his culinary skills and his love for experimenting with flavors. We sampled the beetroot carpaccio, fried chicken wings, lamb burger, and pan-seared trout fish, each dish crafted with attention to detail. Paired with some Belgian ale, it made for a truly satisfying meal.

To balance all this modern flair, we then visited Chopsticks, one of the oldest and most reliable places in Manali. Known for hearty Tibetan fare, this stop was all about comfort. A steaming bowl of mixed gyathuk, with its broth rich in flavor and noodles perfectly cooked, was just the kind of soulful food one craves in the mountains.

We couldn’t resist a sweet detour at Jeet Sweet Shop, an old-style mithai shop tucked into the town. Walking in felt like stepping back in time, with trays lined with traditional sweets that have been part of Manali’s food culture for generations. We tasted their khoye ki burfi, dal ki burfi, nariyal ki burfi, along with besan ki burfi, crispy namak pare, and sev buniya. Each bite carried the charm of recipes that haven’t changed in decades.

The food tour came to a fitting close at Kachnar Restaurant, where we were served a curated Himachali meal. The spread included chha gosht, a mutton curry cooked in yogurt-based gravy, and Himachali kukkad curry, both paired with hot tandoori rotis. The meal ended on a sweet note with meetha bhat, a fragrant sweet rice dish. 
This journey through Old Manali’s cafés and kitchens was more than just about food, it was about the people, their stories, and the way flavors from around the world have found a home in this mountain town.
